seo.title: MCP Notifications — Stop Your Tool Looking Frozen
altTitles: MCP Progress And Logging In One Chapter
seo.hook: Thirty seconds of silence. Working, or dead?
seo.breakdown: the two server calls that report progress, the two client callbacks that catch them, and why they go in different places

scenes.narration: A tool that runs for thirty seconds and says nothing looks broken.
Two calls fix that, one more lets the person stop it, and by the end you'll know which of them the spec has already deprecated. Learn MCP, on THE NBX STUDIO.

On the server side there're exactly two calls worth knowing, and they do different jobs. C t x dot info sends a log line — a human sentence about what's happening right now. Searching Wikipedia, for instance. C t x dot report progress sends a number instead: how far through, out of how much. Thirty out of a hundred. As the work moves on you send more of both, writing report, and eighty percent. Neither call changes what the tool returns, because they're side channels that travel while the tool is still running — which is exactly why they're useful.

scenes.narration: On the client side you'll write two callbacks, and where each one's registered is the detail people get wrong. The logging callback goes on the session, because log messages can arrive from anything the server's doing, not just the tool you happen to be waiting on. The progress callback goes on the individual call tool, because progress belongs to one specific piece of work — thirty percent of what, otherwise? Register them both and your interface can show a spinner with real text and a bar with a real number, instead of a frozen window and a user reaching for the close button.

scenes.narration: Progress solves half the problem. Here's the other half, and the spec lists it as a core utility alongside progress: cancellation. If a request can run for thirty seconds, the person watching needs a way to stop it — otherwise your only honest option is making them wait for something they no longer want. When the client cancels, your tool's async task is cancelled underneath you, so the shape that saves you is an ordinary try and finally: clean up whatever you opened, then let the cancellation propagate. Swallowing it is the mistake — catch and ignore, and you've built a tool nobody can stop. And if the work is genuinely long, minutes rather than seconds, that's what the Tasks extension is for: it hands back a durable handle you poll, instead of holding a request open and hoping.

scenes.narration: One caveat, and it splits this chapter in two. Progress reporting is current, healthy, and listed in the spec as a core utility — report progress is not going anywhere. The logging half is deprecated, in the same twenty twenty six revision as sampling and roots. If you're on stdio, the guidance is to write to standard error instead, which the client already captures; and for anything you'd actually operate in production, use Open Telemetry, which is built for exactly this and gives you traces rather than loose strings. So keep report progress, and treat c t x dot info as something you'll meet in existing code rather than something to build on.
